children: The Reserve Bank of India is likely to continue using temporary liquidity absorption tools such as variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions and dollar-rupee buy-sell swaps to manage surplus liquidity, after refraining from announcing a cash reserve ratio (CRR) hike or fresh open market operation (OMO) sales in its October 7 policy review, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said during the post-policy press conference.

Dealers expect the central bank to announce an OMO sales calendar of around Rs 1 lakh crore, while VRRR auctions and foreign exchange swaps are likely to remain key tools for absorbing surplus liquidity.

“On liquidity, the absence of a CRR hike and OMO sale suggests that the RBI is comfortable continuing with VRRRs, buy-sell swaps and ongoing sterilisation,” said VRC Reddy, General Manager and Head of Treasury at Karur Vysya Bank.
Malhotra, however, said the central bank does not expect the current surplus liquidity conditions to persist for long and left the door open to using CRR or other measures if required.

“On liquidity, there is surplus liquidity, much more than the liquidity that is required, but we believe that this is not a very long-term phenomenon,” Malhotra said at the post-policy press conference.
He said natural factors such as currency leakage, banks’ reserve requirements and the RBI’s foreign exchange operations would gradually absorb a substantial part of the surplus.
“Within this financial year itself, I expect a large amount of this liquidity without giving numbers. Three-four lakh crore rupees is generally the currency leakage that happens,” Malhotra said.
He added that the RBI’s sell-buy swaps, OMO operations, VRRR auctions and spot intervention to support the rupee would also help absorb liquidity.
CRR remains an option
The Governor’s comments also suggest that the RBI has not ruled out a more durable liquidity absorption measure such as a CRR increase, even though it did not announce one in the October policy.
Asked whether CRR was off the table given that FX swaps are more expensive for the RBI, Malhotra said the central bank would not rule out any option.
“I would not rule out anything because it is still an evolving and an uncertain world,” he said.

System liquidity had increased substantially during August and September following measures undertaken to attract capital inflows. The net position under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) showed an average daily surplus of Rs 5.9 lakh crore since the previous MPC meeting in August. According to the RBI’s latest data, the liquidity surplus stood at Rs 4.93 lakh crore on Tuesday.

The sharp increase was largely driven by capital inflows following special measures introduced by the RBI, including the facility to attract foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits. The RBI responded with VRRR auctions and OMO bond sales to absorb the excess. These measures, along with quarterly advance tax outflows, moderated the surplus in September.
Liquidity to remain in surplus
Madhavi Arora, Chief Economist at Emkay Global Financial Services, said system liquidity is likely to remain in surplus even as the RBI tightens liquidity conditions.

“From a signalling perspective, while the policy rate and liquidity stance will both incrementally tighten ahead, system liquidity is likely to remain above 1 percent of NDTL by end-March 2027, even with RBI’s liquidity absorption in coming months. We maintain a cumulative rate hike of 75 basis points in this cycle, but will be watchful of the fluid global dynamics,” she said.

The RBI said surplus liquidity had pushed the weighted average call rate (WACR) towards the lower half of the policy corridor. Short-term money market rates, particularly commercial paper and certificates of deposit, also moderated significantly during August and September.
At the same time, government securities yields hardened from mid-August to September amid renewed geopolitical tensions in West Asia, higher global bond yields and rising crude oil prices.
Lakshmanan V, Group President and Head-Treasury (Treasurer) at Federal Bank, said the RBI had left enough room to act depending on liquidity conditions.
“On the liquidity measures too, RBI left enough room for them to act based on the need,” he added.
For now, the focus will remain on VRRR auctions, FX swaps and the expected OMO sales calendar, while CRR remains an option if surplus liquidity does not ease as expected.

title: RBI keeps liquidity tools flexible as surplus seen easing by March
